pieces.text: Sectionalism means supporting one's own
, or region, over the whole country. So, these choices are correct:

content.text: a Wisconsin merchant who helps organize a local chapter of a political party that only represents Northern voters

explanationText.text: Because the political party prioritizes Northern interests, this is an example of sectionalism.

content.text: a Mississippi slaveholder who supports low tariffs that benefit Southern agriculture but harm the development of Northern factories

explanationText.text: Because the slaveholder is prioritizing Southern economic interests over Northern ones, this is an example of sectionalism.

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: a Connecticut factory owner who works closely with Southern slaveholders to get cotton for his fabric-making business

explanationText.text: Because this person profits from cooperating with people in the South, including slaveholders, this is not an example of sectionalism.

content.text: a North Carolina congressman who supports Southern slavery but would rather the government focus on what he thinks are more important national issues

explanationText.text: Because this congressman prioritizes national issues over Southern slavery, this is not an example of sectionalism.

. Read about the Wilmot Proviso. Then answer the question below.

. Read about the Wilmot Proviso. Then follow the instructions below.

contents.text: A month before the Civil War began, Abraham Lincoln was inaugurated as president. In his inaugural address, he directly addressed Southern states, some of which had already seceded from the Union. Read the excerpt from his address. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Apprehension seems to exist among the people of the Southern states that by the [election] of a Republican administration their property and their peace and personal security are to be endangered.…I declare that I have no purpose, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the institution of slavery in the states where it exists. I believe I have no lawful right to do so, and I have no inclination to do so….

[No] state upon its own mere motion can lawfully get out of the Union;…[resolutions] and ordinances to that effect are legally void, and…acts of violence within any state or states against the authority of the United States are [rebellious] or revolutionary, according to circumstances.

I therefore consider that in view of the Constitution…the Union is unbroken, and to the extent of my ability, I shall take care, as the Constitution itself expressly enjoins upon me, that the laws of the Union be faithfully executed in all the states.…

In your hands, my dissatisfied fellow-countrymen, and not in mine, is the momentous issue of civil war. The government will not assail you. You can have no conflict without being yourselves the aggressors.

contents.text: Read the passage about the Battle of Fort Sumter. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Starting in December 1860, South Carolinian troops began to seize several U.S. Army forts around Charleston. Unable to defend the forts, U.S. Army Major Robert Anderson and his garrison retreated to Fort Sumter. These troops held the fort for the next three months but were unable to receive supplies due to a Confederate blockade in Charleston Harbor.

In April 1861, Confederate General P. G. T. Beauregard demanded that Anderson surrender the fort, threatening to attack it if he did not. Anderson ignored Beauregard's warning, and on April 12, Confederate forces bombarded the fort with cannon fire, the first shots of the Civil War. Although the garrison lost no men, the fort's walls were damaged. Anderson's troops were forced to abandon the fort to the Confederacy.

After hearing of Fort Sumter's capture, President Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to form an army in order to put down the rebellion in the Confederacy. However, believing that Lincoln's call was a declaration of war on the entire South, four more states—Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee—voted to secede from the Union and join the other seven states of the Confederacy.

contents.text: Read the passage about the Battle of Fort Sumter. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Starting in December 1860, South Carolinian troops began to seize several U.S. Army forts around Charleston. Unable to defend the forts, U.S. Army Major Robert Anderson and his garrison retreated to Fort Sumter. These troops held the fort for the next three months but were unable to receive supplies due to a Confederate blockade in Charleston Harbor.

In April 1861, Confederate General P. G. T. Beauregard demanded that Anderson surrender the fort, threatening to attack it if he did not. Anderson ignored Beauregard's warning, and on April 12, Confederate forces bombarded the fort with cannon fire, the first shots of the Civil War. Although the garrison lost no men, the fort's walls were damaged. Anderson's troops were forced to abandon the fort to the Confederacy.

After hearing of Fort Sumter's capture, President Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to form an army in order to put down the rebellion in the Confederacy. However, believing that Lincoln's call was a declaration of war on the entire South, four more states—Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee—voted to secede from the Union and join the other seven states of the Confederacy.

textContent.text: Copperheads opposed the war for several reasons. Many held racist views and did not think Black Americans deserved freedom, citizenship, or equal rights. Others believed preserving the Union wasn't worth the massive loss of life. In places like Ohio and Indiana, linked with the South by trade, many opposed a war that brought economic hardship.

rallied support by denouncing President Lincoln. Antiwar sentiment contributed to a violent reaction against the 1863 Union military draft. textContent.text: Nearly all Copperheads supported the Democratic Party, which tended to support Southern and rural interests. Others believed preserving the Union wasn't worth the massive loss of life. In places like Ohio and Indiana, linked with the South by trade, many opposed a war that brought economic hardship.

pieces.text: Opposition to the war took many forms. Copperhead newspapers such as the

rallied support by denouncing President Lincoln. Antiwar sentiment contributed to a violent reaction against the 1863 Union military draft. In New York City, a protest against the draft escalated into a deadly riot, during which white mobs destroyed property and murdered hundreds of people, targeting the city's Black population.

textContent.text: Nearly every Northerner who opposed the war supported the Democratic Party, which tended to support Southern and rural interests. Their candidates favored a treaty with the Confederacy that granted it independence or supported reunification with constitutional protections for slavery. They believed a Democratic win in the 1864 presidential election could end the war. The party nominated George B. McClellan, a popular Union general, for president. Even though McClellan supported the war, Copperheads believed he was the Democratic Party's only hope of defeating Lincoln.

contents.text: Match each excerpt from a soldier's account to the reason it shows for fighting in the Civil War.

Many Northerners fought to end the institution of slavery across the country.

contents.text: When the Civil War began, almost 90 percent of the 4 million Black Americans were enslaved. The war provided unique opportunities for many Black people, even before millions of those enslaved were freed by the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. However, the war also presented notable challenges.
Sort each statement by whether it reflects an opportunity or a challenge for Black Americans during the Civil War.

label.text: Military service by Black Americans helped convince many people that they deserved full political equality.
After the Emancipation Proclamation made ending slavery a goal of the war, some white Northerners blamed Black people for the death of white soldiers.
After emancipation, Black women working as teachers and nurses in the South helped formerly enslaved people build new communities.
For most of the war, Black soldiers were paid less than white soldiers and often given low-status jobs.
Free Black people could serve in the Union military, while those still enslaved could serve as Union army informants and scouts.
Rather than allowing Black soldiers to surrender in battle, many Confederate commanders executed or re-enslaved them.

contents.text: During the Civil War, women had no voting rights and little political voice. At the time, the private home was viewed as the primary area of women's influence. However, the challenges of the war allowed women to participate in life outside the home in a variety of ways. Match each challenge of war with the way women responded.

draggableItems.text: Reformers such as Clara Barton, Elizabeth Blackwell, and Dorothea Dix helped train women to be nurses and organized the delivery of medical supplies.
In Richmond, VA, poor women broke into shops in search of food and clothing, an event later called the Richmond Bread Riot.
Women learned how to manage businesses and farms and took on roles in factories or government.
Hundreds of women are estimated to have disguised themselves as men to serve in battle, and more served unofficially as spies.

staticItems.text: Military hospitals and camps did not have enough trained staff to deal with the unprecedented number of wounded soldiers.
Under Union and Confederacy laws, women were not allowed to serve in the military.
Environmental destruction due to the war caused the prices of food and basic necessities to skyrocket, especially in the South.
Millions of Northern and Southern men left the workforce to join the military and fight.

, and
. These groups had been forcibly relocated from the Southeast during the 1830s and 1840s.

Many Northerners fought to end the institution of slavery across the country.

contents.text: When the Civil War began, almost 90 percent of the 4 million Black Americans were enslaved. The war provided unique opportunities for many Black people, even before millions of those enslaved were freed by the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863. However, the war also presented notable challenges.
Decide whether each statement reflects an opportunity or a challenge for Black Americans during the Civil War.

questions.text: For most of the war, Black soldiers were paid less than white soldiers and often given low-status jobs.
After emancipation, Black women working as teachers and nurses in the South helped formerly enslaved people build new communities.
After the Emancipation Proclamation made ending slavery a goal of the war, some white Northerners blamed Black people for the death of white soldiers.
Military service by Black Americans helped convince many people that they deserved full political equality.

, after the venomous snake. Read the passage about Northern opposition to the war. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Copperheads opposed the war for several reasons. Many held racist views and did not think Black Americans deserved freedom, citizenship, or equal rights. Especially after the Emancipation Proclamation, Copperheads feared that newly freed people would move to the North and destroy its racial order that benefited white Northerners. Others believed preserving the Union wasn't worth the massive loss of life. In places like Ohio and Indiana, linked with the South by trade, many opposed a war that brought economic hardship.

pieces.text: Opposition to the war took many forms. Copperhead newspapers such as the

rallied support by denouncing President Lincoln. Antiwar sentiment contributed to a violent reaction against the 1863 Union military draft. In New York City, a protest against the draft escalated into a deadly riot, during which white mobs destroyed property and murdered hundreds of people, targeting the city's Black population.

textContent.text: Nearly every Northerner who opposed the war supported the Democratic Party, which tended to support Southern and rural interests. Their candidates favored a treaty with the Confederacy that granted it independence or supported reunification with constitutional protections for slavery. They believed a Democratic win in the 1864 presidential election could end the war. The party nominated George B. McClellan, a popular Union general, for president. Even though McClellan supported the war, Copperheads believed he was the Democratic Party's only hope of defeating Lincoln.

draggableItems.text: Military hospitals and camps did not have enough trained staff to deal with the unprecedented number of wounded soldiers.
Under Union and Confederacy laws, women were not allowed to serve in the military.
Environmental destruction due to the war caused the prices of food and basic necessities to skyrocket, especially in the South.
Millions of Northern and Southern men left the workforce to join the military and fight.

staticItems.text: Hundreds of women are estimated to have disguised themselves as men to serve in battle, and more served unofficially as spies.
Women learned how to manage businesses and farms and took on roles in factories or government.
Clara Barton, a Northern reformer, worked for the Union army to deliver medical supplies and set up hospitals near the front lines.
In Richmond, Virginia, poor women broke into shops in search of food and clothing, an event later called the Richmond Bread Riot.

pieces.text: Nearly 3 million Americans fought in the Civil War—about 2 million for the Union and more than
for the Confederacy. Soldiers on both sides fought for a variety of reasons, many of which are revealed in the personal accounts they kept, including diaries, letters, and memoirs.

contents.text: Match each excerpt from a soldier's account to the reason it shows for fighting in the Civil War.

draggableItems.text: Many soldiers fought out of a sense of patriotic duty to their country.
Many Southerners fought to protect the institution of slavery in the South.
Many Northerners fought to end the institution of slavery across the country.
Many poor Southerners were drafted, or forced to fight, by the Confederate government, while rich planters were exempt.

staticItems.text: This country without slave labor would be completely worthless….We can only live and exist by that species of labor: and hence I am willing to fight to the last.—William Nugent, Mississippi

I could be at home if it weren't for a few big rulers who I cannot help but blame for it.…They lay at home feasting on the good things of the land…while we poor soldiers are forced away from home.—James Zimmerman, North Carolina
Dear wife…I am a soldier now and I shall use my utmost endeavor to strike at the rebellion and the heart of this system [of slavery] that so long has kept us in chains.—Samuel Cabble, Massachusetts
While duty calls me here and my country demands my services I should be willing to make the sacrifice.…—Henry Crydenwise, New York
